Issues of [[heterogeneity]] in [[duration models]] can take on different forms. On the one hand, unobserved heterogeneity can play a crucial role when it comes to different [[sampling methods]], such as [[Stock sampling|stock]] or [[flow sampling]].<ref>	 Salant, S. W. (1977): Search Theory and Duration Data: A Theory of Sorts. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 91(1), pp. 39-57</ref>  On the other hand, duration models have also been extended to allow for different [[subpopulations]], with a strong link to [[mixture models]]. Many of these models impose the assumptions that heterogeneity is [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] of the observed [[covariates]], it has a [[Probability distribution|distribution]] that depends on a finite number of [[parameters]] only, and it enters the [[hazard function]] [[multiplicatively]].<ref>	 Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass.</ref>

One can define the conditional hazard as the hazard function conditional on the observed covariates and the unobserved heterogeneity.<ref>	 Lancaster, T. (1990): The Econometric Analysis of Transition Data. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref>  In the general case, the [[cumulative distribution function]] of ''t<sub>i</sub>*'' associated with the conditional hazard is given by ''F(t|x<sub>i</sub> , v<sub>i</sub> ; θ)''. Under the first assumption above, the unobserved component can be integrated out and we obtain the cumulative distribution on the observed covariates only, i.e.

''G(t ∨ x<sub>i</sub> ; θ , ρ) = ∫ F (t ∨ x<sub>i</sub>, ν ; θ ) h ( ν ; ρ ) dν'' <ref>	 Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass.</ref>

where the additional parameter ρ parameterizes the density of the unobserved component ''v''. Now, the different estimation methods for stock or flow sampling data are available to estimate the relevant parameters.

A specific example is described by Lancaster. Assume that the conditional hazard is given by

''λ(t ; x<sub>i</sub> , v<sub>i</sub> ) = v<sub>i</sub> exp (x <ref>i</ref> β) α t <sup>α-1</sup>''

where ''x'' is a vector of observed characteristics, ''v'' is the unobserved heterogeneity part, and a [[normalization (statistics)|normalization]] (often E[''v<sub>i</sub>''] = 1) needs to be imposed. It then follows that the average hazard is given by exp(x'β) αt<sup>α-1</sup>. More generally, it can be shown that as long as the hazard function exhibits proportional properties of the form ''λ ( t ; x<sub>i</sub>, v<sub>i</sub> ) = v<sub>i</sub> κ (x<sub>i</sub> ) λ<sub>0</sub> (t)'', one can identify both the covariate function ''κ''(.) and the hazard function ''λ''(.).<ref>	 Lancaster, T. (1990): The Econometric Analysis of Transition Data. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref>

Recent examples provide a [[nonparametric]] approaches to estimating the baseline hazard and the distribution of the unobserved heterogeneity under fairly weak assumptions.<ref>	 Horowitz, J. L. (1999): Semiparametric and Nonparametric Estimation of Quantal Response Models. Handbook of Statistics, Vol. 11, ed. by G. S. Maddala, C. R. Rao, and H. D. Vinod. North Holland, Amsterdam.</ref>  In [[grouped data]], the strict [[exogeneity]] assumptions for time-varying covariates are hard to relax. [[Parametric equation|Parametric]] forms can be imposed for the distribution of the unobserved heterogeneity,<ref>	 McCall, B. P. (1994): Testing the Proportional Hazards Assumption in the Presence of Unmeasured Heterogeneity. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 9, pp. 321-334</ref> even though [[semiparametric]] methods that do not specify such parametric forms for the unobserved heterogeneity are available.<ref>	 Heckman, J. J. and B. Singer (1984): A Method for Minimizing the Impact of Distributional Assumptions in Econometric Models for Duration Data. Econometrica, 52, pp. 271-320</ref>
